terms.gloss: slightly, a little (with verbs and prepositions)
evidence: Caes. BG 6.9: paulum suprā eum locum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With verbs and prepositions: paulum differre, to differ slightly; paulum suprā, slightly above. With a comparative Latin uses the ablative paulō instead (next). The same word is the noun “a little” of an amount (see a little).

terms.grammar: ablative of the degree of difference, with a comparative or with ante, post
evidence: Cic. Quinct. 11: paulō minus cōnsīderātus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin measures the difference by the ablative: paulō major, slightly bigger; paulō ante, a little earlier (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.83: quī leviter aegrōtantēs lēniter cūrant (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of a condition that is slight, not grave: leviter aegrōtāre, to be slightly ill; leviter saucius, slightly wounded. This is its usual sense in Cicero; the literal “lightly, not heavily” is rare (Lewis & Short).

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Ter.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra
evidence: Ter. And. 447: Subtristis vīsus est esse aliquantulum mihi.
terms.comment: Latin can say “slightly” with the prefix sub-: subtristis, a little sad, is Terence’s (Lewis & Short: ante- and post-classical). Use the compounds the dictionary gives rather than coining new ones.

phrases.english: (doctors) who treat the slightly ill gently

phrases.latin: Subtristis vīsus est esse aliquantulum mihi.
phrases.english: He seemed to me a little on the sad side.
